headline: A 2015 federal law expanding anti-trafficking penalties, victim services, grants, and related rules across criminal justice, health, immigration enforcement, and child welfare.
what_it_does: The law adds a $5,000 assessment on people and entities convicted of certain sex, slavery, trafficking, and smuggling crimes, with the money going to a Domestic Trafficking Victims' Fund that pays for anti-trafficking grants and victim services. It makes several changes to how trafficking victims get services, creates grant programs for states and localities, makes buyers of commercial sex subject to prosecution, and adds rules for missing children reports and crime victims' rights. It also creates a Cyber Crimes Center within Immigration and Customs Enforcement, expands sex offender registry reporting for military members, and sets up training requirements for federal workers, health care staff, and Homeland Security personnel.

who_it_affects.group: People convicted of trafficking, sexual abuse, child exploitation, or certain smuggling offenses
who_it_affects.how: They may owe an extra $5,000 assessment, payable only after other court-ordered fines, restitution, and victim compensation are paid.

U.S. citizens and permanent residents who are victims of severe trafficking can get victim benefits without first getting HHS certification, and victims may receive restitution from forfeited property.

who_it_affects.group: State and local governments and law enforcement
who_it_affects.how: They can apply for Justice Department grants for anti-trafficking training, task forces, and child trafficking programs, and they may get funding preferences if their state has certain laws in place.

who_it_affects.group: People who buy commercial sex acts
who_it_affects.how: They can be prosecuted for patronizing or soliciting people for commercial sex acts in sex trafficking cases.

who_it_affects.group: Runaway and homeless youth and their service providers
who_it_affects.how: Youth who have experienced trafficking are added as an eligibility factor for certain grants for runaway and homeless youth services.

who_it_affects.group: Missing children's families and foster care agencies
who_it_affects.how: State missing-child reports must include a recent photo when available, and records must be verified within 30 days instead of 60.

who_it_affects.group: Military members required to register as sex offenders
who_it_affects.how: The Defense Department must send registration information for certain released or sentenced service members to the national sex offender registry.
HHS funds training programs to help clinicians recognize and respond to trafficking victims.
Trafficking victims can join Job Corps without showing low-income eligibility.
The HERO Child Rescue Corps program is set up to recruit and hire wounded, ill, or injured veterans for child exploitation investigation roles.
They must be notified of plea bargains and deferred prosecution agreements in a timely way and given information on the DOJ Victims' Rights Ombudsman.

who_it_affects.group: Grant recipients and nonprofit organizations receiving Justice Department grants
who_it_affects.how: They face annual Inspector General audits, a ban on certain offshore-account nonprofits, limits on conference spending, and a ban on lobbying DOJ or state and local officials about grant awards.

when_it_takes_effect: Enacted May 29, 2015; several provisions apply starting with fiscal years 2015 through 2016, and some grant authorities and the $5,000 assessment run through fiscal year 2019 or 2020.
